title: Loving By God's Word
subtitle: 1 Corinthians 13 is a definition, and every item on it is something you do.
objectives: State the greatest commandment from Matthew 22:37-39
List what 1 Corinthians 13 says love is and is not
Explain why love is described in verbs rather than feelings
Explain the new command in John 13:34-35
Apply one of the descriptions to a real situation

cards.title: Somebody asked which rule was the biggest
cards.text: Jesus answers with two, and says everything else hangs on them. Matthew 22, verses 37 to 39.

cards.title: Two commands, in that order
cards.text: Love God with all your heart, soul and mind. And love your neighbour as yourself.
points: **The first is about direction.**
**The second is about everyone in front of you.**
**"As yourself"** is the measure given.
**Everything else** is said to hang on these two.

question.text: What are the two greatest commandments?
options: Pray daily, and read the Bible
Love God, and love your neighbour as yourself
Do not steal, and do not lie
Honour your parents, and tell the truth
question.explain: Matthew 22:37-39. Jesus says everything else in the law hangs on those two.

cards.title: The definition nobody expects
cards.text: It is read at weddings, but it was written to a church that was arguing. Every item in it is a behaviour.
points: **Love is patient. Love is kind.**
**It does not envy or boast.** It is not proud.
**It keeps no record of wrongs.**
**Not one of those is a feeling.**

cards.title: It is written entirely in verbs
cards.text: Paul could have described a feeling. He lists actions instead, which means the passage can be checked against a real day.
points: **A feeling cannot be measured.** A behaviour can.
**"Keeps no record of wrongs"** is testable.
**Verbs are why the chapter is useful.**
**Same reason a character is judged on deeds.**

question.text: Which of these does 1 Corinthians 13 say about love?
options: It keeps no record of wrongs
question.explain: It is a list of behaviours: patient, kind, not envious, not proud, keeping no record of wrongs.

cards.title: Good spot to pause
cards.text: Part 2 is the new command, and what makes it new. Your place is saved.

cards.title: Why call it new when it was already there?
cards.text: Loving your neighbour was in the law already. In John 13 Jesus adds something to it, and that addition is the change.

cards.title: As I have loved you
cards.text: The old measure was "as yourself". The new one is "as I have loved you", which is a much harder standard.
points: **"As yourself"** — a measure you already know.
**"As I have loved you"** — an example instead.
**And people will know you by it**, he says.
**Not by what you say you believe.**

cards.title: A standard you can see beats a rule you are told
cards.text: A coach who shows you the movement teaches faster than a coach who describes it. That is the difference between the two versions.
points: **"As yourself"** is a rule you have to interpret.
**"As I have loved you"** is a demonstration.
**You can copy a demonstration.**
**That is why it is called new.**

question.text: What makes the command in John 13:34 new?
options: It is the first time love is mentioned
The measure changes from "as yourself" to "as I have loved you"
question.explain: Loving your neighbour was already in the law. The standard is what changes.

cards.title: Patience is the stat nobody levels up
cards.text: Patient is the first word on the list. It gets tested by ordinary annoying things, not by big events.
points: **Small, repeated, unglamorous.**
**Nobody notices it working.**
**Everybody notices it missing.**
**It is trainable.** That is the useful part.

cards.title: Pick one and check it against today
cards.text: The chapter is only useful if you hold it against something real, which is uncomfortable and is the point.
points: **Was I patient with the person who annoyed me?**
**Did I keep a record of a wrong?**
**Did I boast about something small?**
**One item, honestly**, beats all fifteen vaguely.

question.text: 1 Corinthians 13 describes love mainly as a feeling.
question.explain: False. Every item on the list is a behaviour, which is exactly what makes it checkable.

terms.def: Love God with all your heart, soul and mind; love your neighbour as yourself.
The chapter defining love as a list of behaviours: patient, kind, not proud.
The new command: love one another as I have loved you.
The older measure of loving a neighbour, from the law.
The new measure. An example to copy rather than a rule to interpret.
One item from 1 Corinthians 13, and the most testable one.

cards.title: The four that matter
points: **Love God, love your neighbour.** Matthew 22:37-39.
**1 Corinthians 13 is a list of behaviours**, not feelings.
**The new command changes the measure**, not the rule.
**Check one item against one real day.**

quiz.text: What are the two greatest commandments, according to Matthew 22?
options: Do not steal, and do not lie
Pray daily, and give to the poor
Keep the Sabbath, and honour your parents
Love God with everything, and love your neighbour as yourself
quiz.explain: Matthew 22:37-39, and Jesus adds that everything else hangs on those two.
quiz.objective: State the greatest commandment from Matthew 22:37-39

quiz.text: What measure does Matthew 22:39 give for loving a neighbour?
quiz.explain: As yourself. John 13 later raises that standard to 'as I have loved you'.
quiz.objective: State the greatest commandment from Matthew 22:37-39

quiz.text: Which of these does 1 Corinthians 13 say love is?
quiz.explain: Patient and kind are the first two words of the list, and both are things you do.
quiz.objective: List what 1 Corinthians 13 says love is and is not

quiz.text: Which of these does 1 Corinthians 13 say love does NOT do?
quiz.explain: It keeps no record of wrongs. That is the most checkable item on the whole list.
quiz.objective: List what 1 Corinthians 13 says love is and is not

quiz.text: 1 Corinthians 13 describes love mostly as a feeling.
quiz.explain: False. Every item is a behaviour, which is what makes the chapter usable rather than decorative.
quiz.objective: Explain why love is described in verbs rather than feelings

quiz.text: Why does it matter that the chapter is written in verbs?
options: It was the style of the time
A behaviour can be checked against a real day; a feeling cannot
quiz.explain: You can ask whether you were patient today. You cannot audit a feeling the same way.
quiz.objective: Explain why love is described in verbs rather than feelings

quiz.explain: It is read at weddings, but it was addressed to a divided church. That is why it is so practical.
quiz.objective: List what 1 Corinthians 13 says love is and is not

quiz.text: What is the new command in John 13:34?
options: Love one another as I have loved you
Love only those who love you
quiz.explain: The command was already there. The measure is what changes.
quiz.objective: Explain the new command in John 13:34-35

quiz.text: Why is it called a NEW command if loving your neighbour was already in the law?
options: The standard changes from "as yourself" to "as I have loved you"
It applies to a different group of people
It was written in a different language
quiz.explain: A rule you interpret is replaced by an example you can copy. That is the change.
quiz.objective: Explain the new command in John 13:34-35

quiz.text: According to John 13:35, what will people recognise disciples by?
quiz.explain: By the behaviour, not the statement. That is consistent with the whole lesson.
quiz.objective: Explain the new command in John 13:34-35

quiz.text: Which is the most useful way to apply 1 Corinthians 13?
options: Agree that it is a good passage
Take one item and check it honestly against today
quiz.explain: One item honestly beats all fifteen vaguely. The chapter is a checklist, not a poem.
quiz.objective: Apply one of the descriptions to a real situation

quiz.text: "Patient" is the first word on the 1 Corinthians 13 list.
quiz.explain: True, and it is the item tested by ordinary annoying things rather than by big events.

teacher.summary: Week 4 Devotion covers love as the Bible describes it, matching the Term 1 theme. The organising observation is that 1 Corinthians 13 is written almost entirely in verbs, which is what makes it usable: a behaviour can be checked against a real day and a feeling cannot. Noting that the chapter was written to a church that was arguing, rather than for a wedding, does most of the work of resetting how it is read. John 13:34 is handled as a change of measure rather than a new rule — 'as yourself' is something you interpret, 'as I have loved you' is something you copy — which is also why the boxing analogy about demonstration versus instruction fits without being forced. The lesson ends on one honest self-check rather than on all fifteen items.
discussion: Ask him which item on the 1 Corinthians 13 list is hardest for him. The specific answer matters more than the list.
Ask what 'keeps no record of wrongs' would actually look like this week. It is the most testable line in the chapter.
Ask why the passage is written in verbs. Getting to 'because you can check a behaviour' is the point of the first half.
Ask what changes when the measure moves from 'as yourself' to 'as I have loved you'.
teacher.extension: Have him pick one item from the chapter and track it for three days with a simple yes or no each evening. Three days of honest marks teaches more than reading the chapter ten times.
misconceptions: '1 Corinthians 13 is a wedding reading.' It was written to a church that was arguing, which is why it is so practical.
'Love in the Bible means a feeling.' The chapter is a list of behaviours. Not one item is an emotion.
'The new command replaces loving your neighbour.' It changes the measure of it, from 'as yourself' to 'as I have loved you'.
'Being patient is a personality trait you either have or do not.' It is listed first precisely because it is practised.
